notes: Focused v1.9.0 CLI regressions for #75: SIGINT re-raise, structured --json errors and schema compatibility, one-shot CLI testing, the exit-code scheme, Windows behavior, atomic writes, the completions contract, pagination and config explainability, the macOS config-dir footgun, and MYTOOL_DEBUG. Checked against primary sources on 2026-10-27 (Cracauer, the bash manual, POSIX, Microsoft docs, clap_complete 4.6.11, Click 8.5.0, Typer 0.27.3, go-internal 1.16.0). Assertions define the grading rubric; improvement claims require a recorded harness run against one immutable skill hash. Status (2026-10-27): recorded. Baseline and with-skill runs on Claude Code and Codex, three repetitions per case, are in evals/results/v1.9.0-claude-comparison/ and evals/results/v1.9.0-codex-comparison/ against skill tree 164c1aefd956.

evals.name: sigint-re-raise
evals.prompt: My Go CLI catches SIGINT, cleans up, and calls os.Exit(130). Users report that Ctrl+C in a shell loop doesn't stop the loop. What's wrong?
assertions: Explains that after catching SIGINT the program should restore the default handler and re-raise SIGINT to itself so the parent sees death by signal
Explains that exit(130) reads as 'handled' to bash, which keeps running the loop or script
Shows the Go approach: signal.Reset(os.Interrupt), then syscall.Kill(syscall.Getpid(), syscall.SIGINT), noting it does not apply on Windows
Does not claim that a plain exit(130) is equivalent to dying from SIGINT

evals.name: json-errors
evals.prompt: I'm adding --json to my CLI. How should failures look when the flag is set, and what are the compatibility rules for the output?
assertions: Writes one compact structured error object to stderr, leaving stdout empty, with a non-zero exit code
Includes a stable machine-readable code that scripts can branch on, separate from the human message
Versions the error object together with the success schema
Says to add fields but never remove, rename, or retype them, and to ignore unknown fields on the consumer side
Uses one document for bounded results and NDJSON for unbounded or streaming results
Emits RFC 3339 UTC timestamps with a Z suffix

evals.name: cli-testing
evals.prompt: How should I test a one-shot CLI written in Go? I mostly care about output and exit codes.
assertions: Tests the built binary as a black box on stdout, stderr, and the exit code
Recommends testscript for Go and notes that `! exec` only asserts a non-zero status, so an exact exit code needs a custom command
Covers the no-TTY case and a NO_COLOR case
Uses golden files for text but not color escapes

evals.name: exit-code-scheme
evals.prompt: What exit codes should my CLI use? I want 0 for success and something for usage errors, plus a few of my own.
assertions: Uses 0 for success, 1 for general failure, and 2 for usage errors
Puts documented domain codes in the 3-123 range and says to document them in --help
Avoids 124-128 and above for its own errors because timeout, xargs, and the shell give them meaning
Notes the exit status is 8 bits, so computed codes must be clamped (exit(256) is success)

evals.name: windows-one-shot
evals.prompt: What changes for a one-shot CLI that also has to run on Windows?
assertions: Says Windows has no SIGPIPE, SIGHUP, or 128+N exit codes and treats a closed pipe as a write error
Says ANSI output requires enabling virtual terminal processing for Go and Rust, colorama in Python, and that Node handles it
Says the shell does not expand globs, so the CLI must
Does not map an unhandled Ctrl+C to exit code 130

evals.name: atomic-writes
evals.prompt: My CLI writes a report file and users sometimes get a truncated file after Ctrl+C or a crash. How do I make that safe?
assertions: Writes to a temp file in the same directory as the target, fsyncs it, and renames it over the target
Explains why the temp file must be on the same filesystem as the target
Mentions setting the final file mode explicitly
Says to exit non-zero and never leave a truncated file at the final path, or to keep an explicit partial name
Notes Windows replace is best effort rather than guaranteed atomic

evals.name: completions-contract
evals.prompt: How should I ship shell completions for my Rust CLI, including dynamic completion of argument values?
assertions: Provides a `completion <shell>` command that prints the script to stdout without writing files
Names install locations: bash user completions directory, zsh `_mytool` on fpath, and fish completions directory
Mentions clap_complete and that its dynamic completion (COMPLETE=<shell>) is still behind an unstable feature
Says dynamic completion runs the binary on every Tab press, so it must be fast, side-effect free, and silent except for candidates

evals.name: pagination-config
evals.prompt: My list command hits a paginated API. How should limits and truncation work, and how can users see where config values come from?
assertions: Gives the list command a documented --limit with a finite default and a way to fetch everything (--paginate or a cursor)
Reports truncation on stderr with the flag that fixes it, and keeps stdout clean
Offers a command that prints each effective config value with its source, as `git config --show-origin` does
Accepts --config and a MYTOOL_CONFIG environment variable

evals.name: macos-config-dir
evals.prompt: I'm using Go's os.UserConfigDir for my CLI's config and a macOS user set XDG_CONFIG_HOME but my tool ignores it. Why?
assertions: Explains that os.UserConfigDir returns ~/Library/Application Support on macOS and ignores XDG_CONFIG_HOME there
Recommends checking an absolute XDG_CONFIG_HOME first and falling back to ~/.config by hand
Notes that other helpers (Rust dirs/directories) behave the same way

evals.name: debug-env-var
evals.prompt: Should my CLI read the DEBUG environment variable to turn on stack traces?
assertions: Recommends a tool-specific variable such as MYTOOL_DEBUG instead of plain DEBUG
Explains that the Node debug package owns DEBUG, so DEBUG=* set for another tool would turn on noisy output in yours
Keeps a --debug flag as the primary switch
